title: Refining a low-cost dermatophyte sampling method to enhance culture purity in resource-limited clinical settings in Bangladesh
author: Hasan, Ahmed, et al.
materials: We acknowledge that the collection conditions were not ideal and that environmental control was limited. However, these conditions reflect the true representation of clinical practice in government general hospitals in Bangladesh. The study therefore proposes and evaluates a sampling approach specifically designed to improve culture recovery under such real-world, resource-limited conditions. Overall, method 3 consistently outperformed methods 1 and 2 across all analyses, yielding the highest proportion of pure dermatophyte isolates while maintaining the lowest contamination rate and the highest sensitivity. The chi-square analysis showed that these differences are significant, and the odds ratio analysis highlighted the considerable benefit of method 3. The increased true-positive detection and lower rate of false negatives further support its diagnostic accuracy. Method 1, although traditionally used, showed the least effectiveness, resulting in low recovery rates and high contamination levels, which undermined its reliability for use in crowded settings. Method 2 showed some improvement, but it didn't have the same level of diagnostic strength as method 3. In method 2, no significant difference in contamination or yield was observed between the pre-heated and non-heated tools. These findings highlight method 3 as a dependable, sensitive, and statistically validated diagnostic sampling approach for the recovery of pure dermatophytes through culture-based outcome assessment. Furthermore, all the methods included here were cost-effective and utilized simple equipment and supplies. Method 3 has been demonstrated to be a practical approach for obtaining consistent, positive, and pure cultures outcomes considering its utilization of basic equipment’s and minimal cost for resource limited clinical settings.

steps.title: Prepare SDCA+CG medium
steps.instruction: Prepare Sabouraud Dextrose Agar with chloramphenicol, supplement with cycloheximide to 125 µg/mL and gentamicin to 0.4 µg/mL (SDCA+CG), dispense into sterile vials and pre‑cool the vials to 4 °C.

substeps.instruction: Make Sabouraud Dextrose Agar with chloramphenicol.
Add cycloheximide to a final concentration of 125 µg/mL.
Add gentamicin to a final concentration of 0.4 µg/mL.
Dispense the agar into sterile vials.
Place the vials in a 4 °C refrigerator to pre‑cool.

steps.title: Collect sample – Conventional method
steps.instruction: Sanitize the lesion periphery with 70 % ethanol, air‑dry 30 s, scrape the active edge 5–10 times with a sterile surgical blade, deposit material onto a sterile glass slide, transfer the slide into a pre‑cooled SDCA+CG vial, and keep the vial refrigerated.

substeps.instruction: Apply 70 % ethanol to the lesion periphery and allow to air‑dry for 30 seconds.
Using a sterile surgical blade, scrape the active edge of the lesion 5–10 times.
Collect the scraped material on a sterile glass slide.
Immediately place the slide into a pre‑cooled (4 °C) SDCA+CG vial.
Transport the vial under refrigeration.

steps.title: Collect sample – Heat‑Assisted method
steps.instruction: Create a sterile zone with a spirit‑lamp flame held 1–2 ft from the sampling area, briefly heat and then cool sterile glass slides and blades, then perform the conventional collection and place the slide into a SDCA+CG vial positioned within the flame zone before refrigeration.

substeps.instruction: Light a spirit‑lamp and hold the flame 1–2 feet away from the sampling area to establish a localized sterile zone.
Pass sterile glass slides and sterile surgical blades through the flame briefly, then allow them to cool.
Sanitize the lesion with 70 % ethanol and air‑dry for 30 seconds.
Scrape the active edge 5–10 times with the pre‑heated blade.
Deposit the material onto the pre‑heated glass slide.
Transfer the slide into a pre‑cooled SDCA+CG vial that is positioned within the flame zone.
Transport the vial under refrigeration.

steps.title: Collect sample – Paper‑Zip method
steps.instruction: Follow the heat‑assisted collection, but after scraping place the specimen onto autoclaved Whatman filter paper instead of a glass slide, fold and seal the paper in a zip‑lock bag, transport at 4 °C (or ambient temperature), and upon receipt place the paper onto SDCA+CG medium inside a biosafety cabinet.

substeps.instruction: Perform the heat‑assisted preparation of slides and blades as described for Method 2.
After scraping, place the specimen onto autoclaved Whatman filter paper (instead of a glass slide).
Fold the filter paper to enclose the specimen.
Seal the folded paper securely in a zip‑lock bag.
Transport the bag at 4 °C or at normal ambient temperature.
In the mycology laboratory, open the bag inside a biosafety cabinet and place the filter paper onto SDCA+CG medium.
Proceed with incubation as described for the other methods.

steps.title: Incubate cultures
steps.instruction: Transport all SDCA+CG vials under refrigeration to the laboratory, incubate at 30 °C for 3–5 days with daily visual checks; once preliminary growth is confirmed, sub‑culture onto SDCA+CG agar plates and incubate an additional 5–7 days to obtain mature colonies.

substeps.instruction: Move the refrigerated vials to the laboratory biosafety cabinet.
Incubate the vials at 30 °C for 3–5 days, inspecting daily for early growth and purity.
When preliminary growth is observed, aseptically transfer material onto SDCA+CG agar plates.
Incubate the agar plates at 30 °C for 5–7 days to allow mature colony development and further testing.

steps.title: Perform macroscopic observation
steps.instruction: After the incubation period, examine each vial with the naked eye, record the outcome (Candida spp., contamination, dermatophytes with or without other fungi, no growth, or pure dermatophytes), then transfer the vial contents to a culture plate for further growth as needed.

description: A potential laboratory-based comparative study was conducted at Noakhali Science and Technology University from March 1, 2025, to May 30, 2025. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Ethics Clearance Committee of Noakhali Science and Technology University. Individuals were enrolled based on a clinical diagnosis of dermatophytosis, characterized by erythematous, scaling lesions with active margins and associated symptoms. Cases of ulceration or those presenting with secondary bacterial infections were excluded from the study. In addition, a written informed consent was obtained from all participants.
